site.about.blurb-1: They fill the corpus and hold the citation bar.
site.about.blurb-2: They turn the corpus into a bet and a build order.
site.about.blurb-3: They own the substrate and the numbers that grade it.
site.about.blurb-4: They hold the voice bar and the visual bar, and they can block a merge.
site.about.blurb-5: They run the loop and hold the budget.
site.about.blurb-6: New here, and nobody has said which function they belong to.
site.about.description-1: x runs product demos, each carrying the research that argues for it. The {{agents}} agents that build them are markdown files in the repo; this page is the roster, and what each one puts on a page.
site.about.does-1: Writes the entity pages and holds the depth ladder. Nothing is promoted past skeleton without a primary citation, and every URL it leans on is counted in the sources ledger.
site.about.does-10: The voice gate. Every reader-visible string on this platform ships past anti-ai-voice, and she can block a merge. Nothing here carries her byline; what she leaves behind are the sentences that are not on the page.
site.about.does-11: Reads the diff before it ships and returns block, ship-with-fix, or approve on the voice axis. Never the author of what it grades — that is the whole point of it being a second agent.
site.about.does-12: The same three verdicts on the Peel axis: tokens instead of hard-coded colour, one focal point per viewport, hierarchy that survives a squint.
site.about.does-2: Refuses the claim that agents replace sellers unless a wage series, a Frey-Osborne-style probability, or an Autor paper is attached to it. Those claims live inside the Auto Marketing Demo entities.
site.about.does-3: Places each new entity in the graph and wires its edges. The topology on a research index is her output, and so is the orphan count under it.
site.about.does-4: Owns the technical architecture page, and will not ship a workflow without a passing eval suite.
site.about.does-5: Cuts the corpus into capabilities and sequences them wedge, core, moat. The layer cards and the order of the roadmap are hers.
site.about.does-6: Names the bet in one sentence and closes with the conditions that kill it. A launch page rests on that argument or it has none.
site.about.does-7: Writes the hook. A launch page opens on a claim a reader can disagree with, and lands on one next action.
site.about.does-8: Holds the visual bar and the diagram bar. Every SVG on an entity page is graded against her skill before it renders.
site.about.does-9: Builds the spine every product inherits: the research engine, the product shell, the registry. This page is its work.
site.about.h2-4: What it is not allowed to forget
site.about.note-1: Equipped by {{SHARED_AT}} roles or more. These are the ones that settle arguments between functions.
site.about.note-2: No agent's doctrine names these. Some are new and no role has picked them up; some outlived the surface they were written for.
site.about.p-1: x runs product demos side by side, and each one carries the research that argues for it: entities on a 0–10 depth ladder, primary sources, a typed graph of how they connect. The order is research, then the demo, then the launch page, because a claim gets on a page only once something a reader can open has earned it.
site.about.p-2: The {{agents}} agents below are markdown files in this repo. A model reads one as its system prompt before it does any work, and the {{skills}} skills are the craft primitives those files equip, one capability per file. What an agent claims to own is one column. What it puts on a page you can open is the other, and {{untraced}} of the {{agents}} put nothing there.
site.about.p-3: They belong to x, not to a product. The same researcher fills Atlas Learn’s corpus and the next product’s; the same two critics read the diff either way. What each product keeps is its own build agent and its own <0>research</0> skill, naming the sources that field trusts and the frontier it has already covered — and its folder is the only place either can write. The <1>do_not_impact_other_product</1> skill states that rule; <2>.githooks/check-product-scope.sh</2> enforces it. The pre-commit hook reads <3>ACTIVE_PRODUCT</3> and rejects a commit that reaches into another product’s files.
site.about.p-4: No product currently keeps agents of its own.
site.about.p-5: {{skills}} skills, one capability each. A skill is how a lesson stops being one agent’s habit and becomes something the next agent inherits. When two roles keep contradicting each other in review, the org writes the coordination down as a skill instead of relitigating it every run. They are grouped here by who carries them.
site.about.p-6: {{memory}} notes under <0>.claude/memory</0>. Each one is a correction made once: a page sent back, a claim that did not hold. It is written down so the next run starts on the far side of it, and an agent reads them before it reads its own doctrine.

site.about.why-2: Owns the KPI tree and the SLA table. Neither has a page on this platform.
site.about.why-3: Hires, sharpens, and retires agents. The roster above is downstream of it; no page is written by it.
site.about.why-4: Owns rollout phases, the RACI, and the weekly commitments. None of that is published here.

site.about.why-7: The agent each product's own build agent derives from, carrying the isolation guardrail: one folder, no reach into another. The three derived agents do the building; nothing on the site is this one's work directly.

site.dashboard.body-1: Each product is an isolated demo with its own workspace, roadmap, and changelog — teams own products behind a hard isolation guardrail.
site.dashboard.body-2: Every product carries a deep-research site: entities on a 0–10 depth ladder, typed cross-links, topology, and cited sources.
site.dashboard.body-3: Leave a wish and it gets a receipt: what you asked for, every reply and status change, the run that worked it if a run did, and what that run cost when it recorded one. Where the wish is kept — a row in that product's own database, or this server's memory until the next restart — is printed on the board, because an ephemeral wishlist that pretends to be durable is worse than none. Design Mode (annotate a page and file what you clicked) is an owner tool: site admins get it everywhere, a product's admins get it inside their product.
site.dashboard.body-4: Manage the site → team → product → workspace hierarchy, and export any product as a portable JSON manifest.
site.dashboard.body-5: Each product answers “is this AI trustworthy?” as seven lenses — honesty, Goodhart-resistance, the relationship, fairness, privacy, security, and grow the human — with the tensions named, disclosed as a datasheet, independently audited, and re-checked as the world moves. The seventh is the deepest: does a year of the tool leave the human more capable on their own, or dependent? Open a product to read its trust story.

site.getstarted.body-1: One sentence is enough. It lands on the product's board with your name on it, and you can watch it move.
site.getstarted.body-2: The work happens on a branch of its own, inside that product only, with the change written up before it starts.
site.getstarted.body-3: Two independent reviewers read the change and a person merges it. You get a receipt naming what it cost.
site.getstarted.body-4: A wish is untrusted text handed to an agent with shell access, so the containment is structural, not a filter: the branch, the scope guardrail, and the two critics are enforced by the pipeline, not remembered by it.
site.getstarted.body-5: Work arrives as a pull request. Nothing reaches your product because an agent decided it was finished.
site.getstarted.body-6: Past your guarantee a wish queues behind everybody's guaranteed work — it is never refused, and the board says where it stands.
site.getstarted.description-1: Say what you want in a sentence; it gets built, reviewed and shipped with a receipt. Tiers guarantee how much gets built a day; nothing is ever refused.
site.getstarted.div-3: Why it is safe to let an agent do this
site.getstarted.p-1: Describe what you want in one sentence. It is built on a branch of its own, reviewed before it ships, and comes back with a receipt: what was asked, what was done, what it cost. Your tier decides how much gets built a day — never whether you may ask.
site.getstarted.p-2: Your tier is a floor: that many wishes get built each day, ahead of the free queue. File more and they still get built — they wait behind everybody’s guaranteed work rather than being turned away. What you buy is where in the queue you start.
site.getstarted.p-3: This deployment is open — nothing is for sale and nobody is asked to subscribe. Wishes are built in the order the board puts them.
site.getstarted.p-4: This deployment has no tiers configured, so nothing is for sale. Wishes are built in the order the board puts them.
site.getstarted.p-5: No delivery time is promised — a tier guarantees how many wishes get built, not when in the day they land. A wish too big for one sitting is split into slices, each reviewed on its own. Free is a $0 subscription and stays free; the card on file is never charged there. Cancel from the billing portal at any time — the tier stops at the end of the period and nothing already built goes away.
site.getstarted.p-6: The demo, and every product you built or were given access to. Each one has its own database, wish board and pages.
site.getstarted.p-7: The demo is open to anyone who signs in. Products you build, or are given access to, appear here once you are in.
site.getstarted.p-8: No product yet. The setup page loads the demo.

Every box is numbered as its card below is, and carries the count of its research entities that have reached the <0>working</0> rung, with the bar along its foot saying the same as a fraction. The <1>working</1> rung is the first that demands a mechanism written down and one number with a dated source under it. Underneath sits the substrate: the layers the flow stands on rather than passes through, carrying only the ties those layers declare for themselves.

A layer sits in tier <0>n</0> when the longest chain of layers under it is <1>n</1> deep, so tier 0 stands on nothing. Every box starts at the same width, and the tinted bar past that mark runs the share of its research entities at the <2>working</2> rung — a mechanism written down, and one number with a dated source under it. The dashed track is what a layer would earn with all of them there. A layer with none has no bar at all. The line above a box is what it promises whatever stands on it.
{{undefended}} — {{v}} no entity underneath carrying a mechanism and a sourced number. The stack still runs. What it cannot do is argue for itself.
Every layer has at least one entity carrying a mechanism and a number with a dated source. The ladder runs two rungs higher than that.

One unit of work, read left to right. Each stage names the promise it makes to the person using the product and the research it rests on, and the entity links go to the page that argues the call. Where the product does not do the thing yet, the stage says so.

The same system read as engineering: what each layer is made of, what it guarantees to the layers standing on it, and the research entity that settled the choice. The stack is grouped by dependency tier, and each layer is drawn as wide as the research it can defend itself with.

That is a statement about the research, not about the market: somebody is competing with this product, and the first job is to name them.

The {{total}} {{v}} this corpus files as a peer, with the evidence each row rests on shown next to it. The rung sits on every row because a comparison assembled out of stubs looks the same as one assembled out of filings, and the difference only shows up when it costs a deal.

A rung badged <0>like this</0> is a rival researched to <1>working</1> whose page also carries a number with a receipt. That is {{rows}} of {{total}} rows: the ones you could quote to a customer without checking them first.

Below <0>working</0> means the page has no mechanism and no number with a receipt: we know the name and roughly the pitch. What those pages are owed clusters, so the fastest route to a comparison that survives a customer quoting it back at us is to clear the top of this list rather than to pick a rival and go deep.

These two pages are what we built out of it: the system cut into layers, each layer naming the promise it makes and the entities it rests on. A layer whose research all sits below the <0>working</0> rung gets flagged, because depth decides what the product may claim.

A depth-7 entity with twelve citations is the wrong shape to post. Each topic here is the same evidence cut down to a few 3:4 cards, a title, a caption and hashtags — in Chinese, sized 1080×1440 for Xiaohongshu. Every card names the entity it came from, so a claim on a card is one you can chase back to a citation.

site.platform.research.sourcesindex.p-1: No cited sources yet. Add citations to entities under <0>app/(products)/{{productSlug}}/research/content/</0>, or seed <1>voices.json</1>, <2>benchmarks.json</2>, <3>incidents.json</3>.
site.platform.research.sourcesindex.p-2: {{pct}} of these citations ({{count}}) point at a DOI or link resolver, which redirects to whoever actually published the work. They are excluded from the ranking below: counting the resolver as a publisher would report a concentration that does not exist. The real publisher of this slice is unknown.
site.platform.research.sourcesindex.p-3: <0>{{publisher}}</0> carries {{pct}} of this corpus ({{count}} of {{citations}} citations). We flag any publisher above 30% for review — a house convention, not a finding, and one that means little when a corpus has few publishers. Either the claims resting on it get a second, independent source, or the pages that lean on it say why no other source exists.
site.platform.research.substratepanels.p: Said in public, by someone who put their name on it.
Each number names the claim it backs. A number that backs nothing is trivia.

site.platform.research.topologygraph.but: Play the growth animation from the first entity to today
site.platform.research.topologygraph.fra: An edge is drawn from the moment both of its entities exist, which is the earliest it could have been wired, not the day it was: all edges share one <0>edges.json</0>, so git can date the edge count but not the individual edge.

This corpus was committed in a single pass: every entity carries the same first-seen date, so the graph is shown whole and there is no cursor. Commit the content across more than one revision and the cursor appears.
site.platform.research.topologygraph.lab: Time cursor — hide entities added after this date
site.platform.research.topologygraph.p-1: , at every position of the cursor
site.platform.research.topologygraph.p-2: Size is prose volume; colour is the depth score <0>as it stands today</0>, on every node{{v}}. Git dates files, not their contents, so what an entity’s depth was on a past date is not recoverable from the log — a node that darkened as time advanced would be an invention. Position comes from a seeded force layout computed at build time: it encodes adjacency and nothing else, so read no meaning into up, down, left or right. Entities that nothing links to sit in the outer belt.{{node}}
